description: Platform-agnostic capability tier for this agent. One-line purpose statement for the agent. Becomes the frontmatter `description` field in the generated agent prompt. Should complete the sentence "This agent..." without starting with "This agent". Be specific about what the agent does, not what it is. "Assesses truth entries against quality dimensions" not "A quality control agent".

Vague descriptions make agents undiscoverable.\n","checks":["Completes the sentence 'This agent...' naturally","Describes what the agent does, not what it is","Specific enough to distinguish from other agents"],"anti_patterns":["Starting with 'This agent' or 'An agent that'","Describing identity instead of action: 'A quality control agent'"],"severity":"warning"}

description: Kebab-case identifier for the agent. Becomes the frontmatter `name` field in the generated agent prompt. Must be unique across all agent definitions. Use descriptive names that communicate domain and function: truth-system-quality-control, not qc-agent.
Human-readable agent title derived mechanically from agent_name. Split on hyphens, capitalize each word. Becomes the frontmatter title field in the generated agent prompt.

Platform-agnostic capabilities to deny even if path grants exist. Each entry is a capability descriptor, not a vendor tool name. Takes precedence over both explicit path grants and auto-derived permissions. Format transformers map capability names to vendor-specific tools.

Platform-agnostic capabilities the agent requests. Each entry is a capability descriptor, not a vendor tool name. A requested capability is only granted if a matching path grant exists and the capability is not prohibited. Format transformers map capability names to vendor- specific tools.

Display label for a context resource. Used in the generated prompt to create readable section headers. "Output Schema", "Canonical Glossary", "Operations Guide". Keep concise — this appears in the agent's prompt.
semantic: {"intent":"Human-readable label that identifies a context resource in the agent prompt. Must be meaningful enough to distinguish resources from each other.\n","checks":["Descriptive enough to identify the resource without seeing its content","Concise — a label, not a sentence"],"anti_patterns":["Generic: 'Context' or 'Data'","Filename repeated as label: 'schema.json'"],"severity":"warning"}

description: Workspace-relative path to a context resource. The transformer uses this to both generate prompt sections (telling the agent about the resource) AND add the path to read hooks (granting access). This dual-purpose mechanism ensures prompt awareness and permission always stay in sync.

Workspace-relative path to a context resource file. The transformer embeds this file's content into the agent prompt as a labeled section (using context_label as the heading) AND adds the path to read hooks (granting file access). This dual-purpose mechanism ensures prompt awareness and permission always stay in sync. Because content is embedded, consider file size — large files consume context window. For context_required, the file must exist at resolution time. For context_available, missing files are silently skipped.

Background execution policy for this agent. Determines how the dispatcher handles this agent's execution lifecycle. 'allowed' means the dispatcher chooses foreground or background based on workload — most common choice. 'required' means the dispatcher must launch this agent as a background process — use for long-running agents that should not block the dispatcher. 'forbidden' means the agent must run in the foreground and the dispatcher waits for completion — use for interactive agents requiring user input.

Tuple of [min, max] records per batch chunk. The dispatcher splits input into chunks of size between min and max. Min must be strictly less than max. Required when dispatch_mode is 'batch'. Example: [50, 100] means each agent invocation gets between 50 and 100 records.
x_constraint: [{"rule":"tuple_ordered","order":"ascending_strict","severity":"error","reason":"First element (minimum batch size) must be strictly less than second element (maximum batch size). A minimum that equals or exceeds the maximum makes the batch size range degenerate.\n"}]

description: How input data reaches the agent. 'file' means the agent reads from a pre-determined file path declared in the definition — also requires security_io_input_file in [security.security_io]. 'directory' means the agent reads from a pre-determined directory path — also requires security_io_input_directory in [security.security_io]. 'tempfile' means the dispatcher writes input to a scoped temp directory and passes the path as parameter — preserves context window for large inputs; also requires security_io_input_tempdir in [security.security_io]. 'inline' means embedded directly in the agent prompt (small inputs only, no file paths or security_io fields needed).

Human-readable description of the input data the agent receives. Describes what the records represent and what the agent does with them. The mechanical format is captured by dispatch_input_format and delivery by dispatch_input_delivery — this field captures domain meaning, but repeating format for human readability is acceptable. Example: "Embedding target records to rewrite and compress to 80-150 characters"

Format of the input data the agent receives. 'jsonl' for newline-delimited JSON records (one per line). 'json' for a single JSON document. 'text' for unstructured text content. This determines how the agent should parse the input file delivered via the delivery mechanism.

Maximum number of concurrent agent instances the dispatcher may spawn. Controls parallelism for batch processing. The dispatcher launches up to this many agents simultaneously, each processing a different chunk. Defaults to 6 if not specified.

How the dispatcher feeds work to the agent. 'batch' means the dispatcher splits input into chunks and invokes the agent once per chunk — requires dispatch_batch_size. 'full' means the dispatcher passes all input at once in a single agent invocation.

Paths granted edit capability from author-defined permissions (System 1). Displayed in Security Boundary section. Maps to platform-specific targeted file modification tools scoped to these paths.

Paths granted read capability from author-defined permissions (System 1). Displayed in Security Boundary section. Maps to platform-specific file read tools scoped to these paths.

Paths granted search capability from author-defined permissions (System 1). Displayed in Security Boundary section. Maps to platform-specific file search and content search tools scoped to these paths.

Paths granted write capability from author-defined permissions (System 1). Displayed in Security Boundary section. Populated by Write fork: when no custom output tool and agent needs disk write access, write=Write becomes an explicit grant here.

Paths granted append capability from system-derived permissions (System 2). NOT displayed to agent. Hooks enforce silently. Covers auto-derived access to log files or accumulation files in temp directories.

Paths granted edit capability from system-derived permissions (System 2). NOT displayed to agent. Hooks enforce silently. Covers auto-derived access to scratch or temp files that require in-place modification.

Paths granted inspect capability from system-derived permissions (System 2). NOT displayed to agent. Hooks enforce silently. Covers auto-derived access to directories containing context or schema files.

Paths granted read capability from system-derived permissions (System 2). NOT displayed to agent. Hooks enforce silently. Covers auto-derived access to context files, schema files, input files, temp directories.

Paths granted search capability from system-derived permissions (System 2). NOT displayed to agent. Hooks enforce silently. Covers auto-derived access to directories containing context or schema files.

Paths granted write capability from system-derived permissions (System 2). NOT displayed to agent. Hooks enforce silently. Covers auto-derived access to scratch temp directories and output temp directories.

Toggle per-group display of individual example headings. When false, examples render as items under the group H3. When true, each example gets its own H4 heading derived from the H2 in the resolved content. Controls detail level without changing content.

Name of the example group, used as the H3 heading when compiling examples into the agent prompt. Groups organize examples by what they demonstrate — "correct rewrite", "incorrect compression", "edge cases".

Heading for an individual example entry. When example_display_headings is true, this becomes the H4 heading for the example in the generated prompt. When derived from @include, the resolver extracts this from the H2 heading in the source .md file.
Inline example text for this entry. Used for short examples that don't warrant a separate .md file. Mutually exclusive with include.

Maximum number of examples to include from this group after include resolution and H2 splitting. Applied AFTER the transformer resolves @include references and splits on H2 boundaries — the count is about resolved individual examples, not raw array entries. Omit to include all examples in the group.

One-sentence statement of what failure means for this agent. Failure refers to the PROCESS, not the DATA. An agent that correctly identifies all inputs as invalid has SUCCEEDED — the assessment process worked. FAILURE means the process itself broke: couldn't read input, couldn't write output, unrecoverable error.
semantic: {"intent":"Defines process failure — not data outcomes. The agent uses this to determine when to report FAILURE vs SUCCESS with bad-data findings.\n","checks":["Describes PROCESS failure, not data quality problems","Specific failure conditions, not 'something went wrong'","Distinguishable from success_definition — no overlap"],"anti_patterns":["Treating bad data as failure ('found invalid entries' is SUCCESS if the process worked)","Restating success_definition in negative form"],"severity":"error"}

description: Observable conditions that prove failure. Each entry is a concrete condition indicating the process broke. "Any record skipped without explanation", "Schema validation failure not resolved after retry", "Output file not created". These are process failures, not data quality findings.
semantic: {"intent":"Process failure detection. The agent checks these conditions to determine whether to report FAILURE instead of SUCCESS.\n","checks":["Each item describes a PROCESS failure condition, not a data quality finding","Each item is observable from the execution environment","Conditions are distinct from success_evidence — no overlap"],"severity":"warning"}

description: Common mistakes to avoid. Each entry describes a specific wrong behavior the agent might exhibit and why it's wrong. "Do not batch-summarize from memory — process each record individually from the source file", "Do not infer missing fields — mark them as absent". Anti-patterns are learned from observed agent failures.
semantic: {"intent":"Calibrates the LLM against its own failure modes. Each item must describe a specific, recognizable mistake — not a generic warning.\n","checks":["Each item describes a specific mistake, not a category of mistakes","Each item is recognizable — agent can detect when it is about to do this","Items are grounded in observed LLM failure modes, not hypothetical risks"],"severity":"warning"}

description: MUST and NEVER rules the agent must follow. Each entry is a single imperative constraint. "MUST validate every record against schema before writing", "NEVER modify source data", "MUST process records in order". Keep constraints specific and verifiable — vague rules get ignored.
semantic: {"intent":"Hard behavioral boundaries in the agent prompt. Violations are agent failures. Each item must be clear enough that both the agent AND a reviewer can determine whether a specific output violates it.\n","checks":["Each item is actionable — agent can determine compliance from the constraint alone","Each item is verifiable — a reviewer can check violation without ambiguity","Items are specific to this agent's failure modes, not generic good practice"],"anti_patterns":["Vague directives: 'be careful', 'ensure quality', 'be thorough'","Constraints the agent cannot actually verify or enforce"],"severity":"warning"}

Opaque directory name (a short slug, not a path) for this agent type's temp staging area. The dispatcher writes input data to /tmp/{workspace}/{value}/ and the agent auto-derives read access to that scoped path. Provide only the name segment — e.g., "cobalt-stage", not "/tmp/myworkspace/cobalt-stage". The format transformer may hash both workspace and value for obfuscation on disk. Must not be derived from the agent name or reveal agent structure — if names follow a predictable pattern, an adversarial LLM can enumerate temp directories for other agent types. Choose an arbitrary, non-descriptive name per agent type. Examples: "cobalt-stage", "theta-7" (good); "embedding-normalizer-input", "input" (bad — reveals agent identity or is too predictable).

description: Prompt instruction telling the agent how to report summary metrics in its return. Composed into the agent prompt when return mode includes metrics. Example: "Include summary metrics with your return: records processed, records passed, records failed."

Instruction indicating what the LLM should use as the filename basis during processing. The LLM derives the identifier from the data being processed. The tool writes to output_directory/{identifier}.{extension}, where the extension is enforced by processing_output_file_format. The LLM controls the filename but not the directory or file type. Example: "{record-identifier}" — the LLM provides a record identifier, the tool writes to the output directory with the correct extension.

How well the output filename is known at definition time. known: exact output file path is declared — also requires security_io_output_file in [security.security_io]. partially: a naming template or instruction constrains the filename but the LLM provides variable parts — also requires security_io_output_directory in [security.security_io], plus processing_output_file_name_template. unknown: completely dynamic, no naming constraint — also requires security_io_output_directory in [security.security_io], plus processing_output_file_name_instruction.

Filename template with {placeholder} syntax for dispatch-time parameters. The tool constructs the output filename by substituting placeholder values provided by the LLM (received as dispatch parameters). The tool controls directory, naming pattern, and extension. The LLM controls only the variable parts. Example: "{interview-id}.summaries.jsonl" — the LLM provides interview-id, the tool constructs the full path.

How to deliver agent-initiated notifications. 'say' uses macOS text-to-speech (good for background monitoring). 'notification' uses macOS Notification Center via osascript (urgent alerts). 'terminal' rings the bell and prints the message. 'log' writes silently to a log file.

Message template for agent-initiated notifications. Can contain {placeholders} the agent fills in at runtime. "{n} of {total} processed, {remaining} remaining". The agent echoes this with a ::notify:: prefix; the hook intercepts and routes to the delivery mechanism.

When to trigger an agent-initiated notification. A human-readable condition the agent evaluates during processing. "every 100 records processed", "on first schema validation failure", "when processing completes". The transformer compiles this into echo instructions in the processing section.

Number of records per write tool call when write frequency is batch. The agent accumulates this many records before invoking the write tool. Balances write frequency against data loss risk from interruption.

Human-readable description of the output data the agent produces. Describes what the output contains and its downstream purpose. Absolute path to the specific file the agent writes its output to. Used in the render schema to specify the resolved output location when the agent produces a single file with a known name.

Output format the agent produces. Prompt instruction telling the agent how to deliver its output data in its return. Composed into the agent prompt when return mode includes output. Example: "Return your output directly as your final message to the dispatcher."

How well the output filename is known at definition time. known: exact output file path is declared — also requires security_io_output_file in [security.security_io]. partially: a naming template or instruction constrains the filename but the LLM provides variable parts — also requires security_io_output_directory in [security.security_io], plus processing_output_file_name_template. unknown: completely dynamic, no naming constraint — also requires security_io_output_directory in [security.security_io], plus processing_output_file_name_instruction.

description: Whether to embed the output schema directly into the agent prompt. When true, the format transformer reads the schema file and inlines its content — uses context window but ensures the agent sees the schema without a tool call. When false (or omitted), the schema path is granted read access and the agent reads it via Read tool — saves context but adds a tool-call round trip. Prefer true for small schemas (under ~100 lines) or when schema adherence is critical. Prefer false for large schemas where context window conservation matters. Either way the agent knows the desired shape.

Number of records per write tool call when write frequency is batch. The agent accumulates this many records before invoking the write tool. Balances write frequency against data loss risk from interruption.

Resolved absolute path to the output directory. Present when the output filename is not fully known at definition time. The enforcement tool writes files within this directory, with filenames constrained by enforcement_output_tool_name_pattern when available.
Resolved absolute path to the output file. Present when the output filename is fully known at definition time. The enforcement tool writes exclusively to this path.

Output format for the enforcement tool. Only present when the agent produces structured output (JSON or JSONL). Text and markdown outputs do not receive enforcement output tools — they use generic write permissions instead.

Whether the LLM must provide a filename when invoking the output tool. Only present when the output filename is not fully known at definition time. When true, the LLM provides a name or identifier that the tool uses to construct the output path within the output directory.

Naming pattern constraint for LLM-provided filenames. Only present when the output filename is partially known — the definition provides a template or instruction and the LLM fills in the variable parts. The tool enforces this pattern when constructing the output path.

Path to the JSON Schema file that validates enforcement tool output. Required for all enforcement output tools — structured output (JSON, JSONL) always requires schema validation. The tool validates each write against this schema before committing to disk.

How often the enforcement tool flushes records to disk. record: one record per write invocation, minimal blast radius. batch: bounded set of records per invocation, size controlled by enforcement_output_tool_batch_size. Only relevant for JSONL — JSON writes the entire file per invocation.

How often the agent flushes records to disk. record: one record per write invocation, minimal blast radius. batch: bounded set of records per invocation, size controlled by processing_output_batch_size. Only relevant for JSONL — other formats write the entire file per invocation by default.
Human-readable description of what a dispatcher parameter represents and how the agent should interpret it. Optional — parameter name and type may be sufficient for self-documenting parameters.

Name of a parameter the dispatcher passes to the agent. This becomes the placeholder name in the agent prompt template. Common names: 'tempfile' (path to input data), 'uid' (record identifier), 'iteration' (processing round number).
Whether this parameter must be provided by the dispatcher. Required parameters cause dispatcher failure if missing. Optional parameters have sensible defaults or conditional behavior.
Type of the parameter value. Used for documentation and dispatcher validation. 'path' for filesystem paths, 'string' for arbitrary text, 'integer' for numeric values, 'boolean' for true/false flags.

Path prefixes granting read-level access. Each entry is a path_allowed_absolute validated against the blocklist. Read-level paths make read, search, and inspect capabilities possible within these paths. Which capabilities are actually granted depends on capabilities_requested intersection.

Path prefixes granting read-level access. Each entry grants recursive access to all files and directories under the prefix. Entries can be workspace-relative (resolved against security_paths_workspace) or absolute. Use relative paths for workspace content (e.g., "schemas/", "definitions/schemas/") and absolute paths for system locations (e.g., "/tmp/"). Read-level paths make read, search, and inspect capabilities possible — actual capabilities granted depend on intersection with security_capabilities_requested.

Path prefixes granting write-level access. Each entry is a path_allowed_absolute validated against the blocklist. Write-level paths make all capabilities possible (write, edit, append, read, search, inspect) within these paths. Which capabilities are actually granted depends on capabilities_requested intersection.

Path prefixes granting write-level access via platform tools (generic write, edit, append). Each entry grants recursive access to all files and directories under the prefix. Entries can be workspace-relative or absolute. Write-level paths make all capabilities possible (write, edit, append, read, search, inspect) — actual capabilities granted depend on intersection with security_capabilities_requested. IMPORTANT: Do not include the agent's output path (security_io_output_file or security_io_output_directory) here — doing so bypasses the enforcement output tool's schema validation and format checking.
Fixed prompt instruction for the metrics portion of the agent return. Composed into the prompt when return_mode includes metrics (status-metrics or metrics-output). Const value — not author-editable.

How the agent returns results to the dispatcher. status: return only SUCCESS or FAILURE. status-metrics: return status plus summary metrics. metrics-output: return metrics plus actual output data. output: return output directly, no status word needed. Determines which return instructions the format transformer composes into the prompt.
Fixed prompt instruction for the output portion of the agent return. Composed into the prompt when return_mode includes output (metrics-output or output). Const value — not author-editable.

Workspace-relative path to a JSON Schema file (must end with .schema.json or .schema.yaml) defining the metric fields the agent returns. Always embedded directly into the prompt — there is no enforcement mechanism for return communication (agent-to-dispatcher LLM text). Embedding ensures the agent sees field names, types, and definitions. Schema file must exist at resolution time. Example: "definitions/schemas/my-agent-return.schema.json"
Fixed prompt instruction for the status portion of the agent return. Composed into the prompt when return_mode includes status (status or status-metrics). Const value — not author-editable.

Expanded role context that builds on role_identity and role_responsibility. Where identity says WHAT you are and responsibility says WHAT you must do, description provides the WHY and HOW — domain context, judgement guidance, and framing that shapes how the agent approaches its work. Optional for simple agents; increasingly valuable as task complexity and required judgement increase.
semantic: {"intent":"Builds the agent's understanding of its role beyond the identity and responsibility. Provides context, nuance, and framing that helps the agent exercise good judgement in ambiguous situations.\n","checks":["Adds context beyond what identity and responsibility already state","Helps the agent understand WHY it does what it does","Appropriate depth for task complexity — simple agents may omit entirely"],"anti_patterns":["Repeating the agent_description verbatim","Restating role_identity or role_responsibility in different words","Generic filler: 'You are a helpful assistant that...'"],"severity":"warning"}

description: Skill and knowledge areas the agent claims. Each entry is a concise phrase describing a competency relevant to the agent's task. These calibrate the LLM's self-model — declare expertise areas that directly support role_responsibility. Typical agents declare 2-5 entries. Be specific: "JSON Schema validation" not "validation", "Gothic linguistic terminology" not "languages". If provided, must contain at least one entry (omit the field entirely rather than providing an empty array). Entries must be unique.

Short noun phrase naming what this agent is. Not a sentence, not a role description — that belongs in role and capabilities. Examples: "semantic quality assessor", "interview summarizer", "embedding normalizer". This becomes the "You are a {identity}" opening in the generated prompt.
semantic: {"intent":"Establishes the agent's behavioral frame. The generated prompt opens \"You are a {role_identity}\" — vague identities produce vague behavior.\n","checks":["Specific enough to distinguish this agent from others in the system","Noun phrase, not a sentence or role description","Names a recognizable specialist, not a generic label"],"anti_patterns":["Generic labels: 'assistant', 'helper', 'processor', 'agent'","Sentences or descriptions instead of noun phrases"],"severity":"error"}

description: One-sentence mandate defining the agent's core obligation. This is the single most important thing the agent must accomplish. Everything else is secondary. Write as a direct imperative: "Assess each truth entry against quality dimensions and produce a structured QC report."
semantic: {"intent":"Defines the agent's primary obligation. Everything else the agent does is secondary to this. A weak responsibility produces unfocused execution.\n","checks":["Single clear mandate, not a list of duties","Written as direct imperative","Specific enough that completion is verifiable","Describes an outcome, not an activity"],"anti_patterns":["Multiple obligations joined by 'and'","Passive voice or vague directives: 'handle', 'manage', 'process'","Describing what the agent IS instead of what it MUST DO"],"severity":"error"}

description: Whether to embed the output schema directly into the agent prompt. When true, the format transformer reads the schema file and inlines its content — uses context window but ensures the agent sees the schema without a tool call. When false (or omitted), the schema path is granted read access and the agent reads it via Read tool — saves context but adds a tool-call round trip. Prefer true for small schemas (under ~100 lines) or when schema adherence is critical. Prefer false for large schemas where context window conservation matters. Either way the agent knows the desired shape.

Path to the JSON Schema file that validates enforcement tool output. Required for all enforcement output tools — structured output (JSON, JSONL) always requires schema validation. The tool validates each write against this schema before committing to disk.

Whether this agent needs a scratch directory for intermediate files. When true, security_io_scratch_tempdir must be provided and the agent auto-derives write access to a scoped temp path. Off by default — most agents keep intermediate state in context. Enable when an agent processes sequential data that loses coherence without file-based checkpointing, or when LLM behavior requires scratch space for processing optimization.
Semantic version string in MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH format. Increment major for breaking changes, minor for new capabilities, patch for fixes.
Prompt instruction telling the agent how to report its completion status in its return. Composed into the agent prompt when return mode includes status. Example: "Return only SUCCESS or FAILURE."

One-sentence statement of what success means for this agent. LLMs are goal-driven — explicit success definitions pull harder than constraints. Write as a positive outcome: "Every input record has been assessed and a valid QC report written to disk."
semantic: {"intent":"The agent's goal state. LLMs are goal-driven — explicit success definitions pull behavior more effectively than constraints push it.\n","checks":["Describes a concrete end state, not an ongoing activity","Refers to the PROCESS succeeding, not data quality outcomes","Observable — you can tell from examining outputs whether this was achieved"],"anti_patterns":["Confusing process success with data quality ('all entries are high quality' is data, not process)","Vague outcomes: 'task completed successfully', 'all items processed'"],"severity":"error"}

description: Observable conditions that prove success. Each entry is a concrete, verifiable statement the agent can check. "Output record count equals input record count", "Every record passes schema validation". These become the agent's self-verification checklist.
semantic: {"intent":"Self-verification checklist. The agent checks each condition after processing to confirm success before reporting.\n","checks":["Each item is a concrete, observable condition — not a subjective judgment","Each item is independently verifiable from outputs alone","Conditions are sufficient — if all pass, success is confirmed"],"severity":"warning"}

description: Absolute filesystem path to the workspace root directory. All workspace-relative paths in the definition (context paths, schema paths, allowed_read/write paths) are resolved relative to this directory. Must be an absolute path (starting with /). Validated against the blocklist during resolution. Any path that resolves outside this workspace or into a blocked zone triggers a SecurityIncident. Example: "/Users/username/.ai/spaces/myproject"
